title: Learn by Doing: Module Two
lead: Module Two sat as a paper: fifty objective questions, then three theory questions with the drawing practicals, each answered as you would write it and then taught from nothing.
intro:
This is the module your Question 2 comes from, and it is the heaviest one. Twenty nine of Test 2's thirty questions were Module Two, and its practical is a drawing: a use case diagram, a data flow diagram or an entity relationship diagram.

How to sit it

Part A, fifty objective questions. All twenty nine Module Two questions from Test 2 first, in the order the examiner set them, then twenty one more chosen to reach as many separate facts as possible.

Part B, three theory questions, one on use cases, one on data flow diagrams and one that pairs fact finding with an entity relationship diagram. Draw every diagram on paper. A diagram you have only read is a diagram you cannot draw.

The habit that earns marks on any of them: the course text gives a numbered procedure for every artefact, and an examiner marking to a scheme is looking for those steps. Write the steps as headings and answer under each. A correct diagram with no working scores less than a correct diagram with its steps labelled.

questions.heading: Actors, include against extend, and the sports centre

scenario.tag: Course text, Module Two Unit 2, pages 71 and 72
scenario.text:
A sports centre offers facilities such as football pitches, tennis courts, basketball courts, and a gym. Customers can book these facilities for specific dates and time slots using an online booking system.
A Customer must first create an account and log in to the system. After logging in, the customer can view available sports facilities, check time slot availability, and make a booking for a preferred facility.
When making a booking, the system displays available time slots. The customer selects a suitable date and time, confirms the booking, and proceeds to make payment. Once payment is successful, the booking is confirmed and recorded in the system. The customer can also view, modify, or cancel bookings. The system sends a booking confirmation notification (via email or SMS) after a successful reservation.
A Staff/Admin manages the system by adding or updating facilities, setting availability schedules, and monitoring bookings. The admin can also generate reports on facility usage and customer bookings.
i. Create a use case diagram for the sports centre booking system in this scenario.
ii. Develop a use case narrative for ANY four use cases in the diagram

questions.asked:
The course text sets the practical. Your paper will put a theory part in front of it, so answer both.

PartWhat to writeMarks
(a)The four types of actor, with a one line definition of each, and how an include relationship differs from an extend relationship in both meaning and notation6
(b i)The use case diagram for the sports centre, showing actors, the boundary, the use cases, and any include or extend relationships6
(b ii)A full use case narrative for Make Booking, and the name, actor and goal of three others5.5

breakdown.question: Which phrases in the scenario are use cases, which are actors, and which one sentence forces an include and which forces an extend?
breakdown.answer:
Actors Customer and Staff/Admin, both named with nouns. Payment and notification are done by outside parties, so a Payment Gateway and a Notification Service are defensible as an external server actor and an external receiver actor.

Use cases Every verb phrase an actor performs: create account, log in, view facilities, check availability, make booking, make payment, view, modify and cancel booking, add or update facility, set availability schedule, monitor bookings, generate reports.

The include "When making a booking, the system displays available time slots", and payment follows every booking. Always, so include.

The extend "The customer can also view, modify, or cancel bookings". Sometimes, and only under a condition, so extend.

Marks The diagram is worth as much as the theory. Draw it properly: boundary rectangle, actors outside, labelled lines.

exam.problem: (a) The four actor types, and include against extend in meaning and notation. (b) For the sports centre booking system: draw the use case diagram, then write a full use case narrative for Make Booking and name three others with their actor and goal.
exam.answer:
(a) The four types of actor.

Actor typeDefinitionExample
Primary business actorPrimarily BENEFITS from the execution of the use case, by receiving something of measurable or observable valueAn employee receiving a salary
Primary system actorDirectly INTERFACES with the system to initiate or trigger a business eventThe bursar who dispenses the cash
External server actorRESPONDS to a request from the use caseThe Financial Director approving the payment
External receiver actorNot the primary actor, but RECEIVES something of measurable value from the use caseA warehouse receiving a packing order

Include against extend.

Include (uses)Extend
MeaningThe base use case ALWAYS requires the other's behaviour. Common functionality reused by several use cases, which promotes reuse and avoids duplicationOptional or conditional behaviour that extends a base use case under specific conditions, extracting complex functionality into its own use case
When it happensAlways, every timeSometimes, only if the condition holds
NotationDashed arrow labelled with the include stereotypeDashed arrow drawn FROM the extension TO the base use case

Both are dashed arrows, so the label and the direction are all that separate them. Read the extend aloud and the arrow makes sense: "Cancel Booking extends Make Booking", so it points back to the base.

(b i) The use case diagram, in the four steps.

Step 1, identify the actors, using the five questions. Who provides input? The customer, and the staff or admin. Who receives output? Both, and the customer receives the notification. Are interfaces required for other systems? Payment is taken and a notification is sent, so a Payment Gateway is an external server actor and a Notification Service is an external receiver actor. Safe answer: Customer and Staff/Admin. Stronger answer: add both external actors and say what type they are.

Step 2, identify the use cases, one verb phrase for each thing an actor does.

CustomerStaff/Admin
Create Account
Log In
View Facilities
Check Availability
Make Booking
Make Payment
View Booking
Modify Booking
Cancel Booking		Log In
Add Facility
Update Facility
Set Availability Schedule
Monitor Bookings
Generate Reports

Step 3, draw the association lines. A boundary rectangle labelled Sports Centre Booking System, with all the use case ovals inside it. The Customer stick figure outside on the left, Staff/Admin outside on the right, Payment Gateway outside on the right of Make Payment. A line from each actor to each use case it takes part in. An arrowhead touching the use case shows the actor initiated it; no arrowhead is used for an external server or receiver actor.

Step 4, identify the include and extend relationships. This is where the marks separate.

  • Make Booking includes Check Availability. Every booking checks availability first, so it is always.
  • Make Booking includes Make Payment. The scenario says the booking is confirmed once payment is successful, so payment happens on every booking.
  • Modify Booking extends Make Booking, and Cancel Booking extends Make Booking. The customer "can also" do these, under a condition, so they are optional behaviour on top of the base.
  • Log In is an include of every use case that requires a logged in customer, since the scenario says the customer must log in first. Login is the standard textbook include.

(b ii) The use case narrative for Make Booking.

PartContent
Name and identifierMake Booking, UC-05
ActorsCustomer (primary system actor), Payment Gateway (external server actor), Notification Service (external receiver actor)
Description and goalThe customer reserves a facility for a chosen date and time slot and pays for it, so that the slot is held in their name
PreconditionsThe customer has an account and is logged in; the facility exists in the system and has an availability schedule set by the admin
Main flow1. The customer selects a facility. 2. The system displays the available time slots. 3. The customer selects a date and time slot. 4. The system reserves the slot provisionally. 5. The customer confirms the booking. 6. The system requests payment through the payment gateway. 7. The gateway returns a successful payment. 8. The system records the booking as confirmed. 9. The system sends a booking confirmation by email or SMS.
Alternative flows3a. No slot is available on the chosen date: the system offers the next available date. 7a. Payment fails or is declined: the system releases the provisional reservation and returns the customer to the payment step. 7b. The slot is taken by another customer while payment is in progress: the system informs the customer and returns to step 2.
PostconditionsThe booking is recorded and confirmed, the time slot is no longer available to other customers, the payment is recorded, and a confirmation notification has been sent

Three more, in brief.

NameActorGoal
Cancel Booking, UC-08CustomerRelease a booking already made, so the slot returns to the pool. Precondition: a confirmed booking exists in the customer's name.
Set Availability Schedule, UC-11Staff/AdminRecord the days and hours for which a facility may be booked. Postcondition: customers can only select slots inside that schedule.
Generate Reports, UC-13Staff/AdminProduce reports on facility usage and customer bookings for a chosen period.

frames.teach: A use case is one complete thing a user gets out of a system, written as a verb phrase: Make Booking, Withdraw Money. A use case DIAGRAM is the picture of who can do what, and it is the first thing you draw once you know the requirements.
frames.ask: In the sports centre, who are the two obvious people that touch the system?

frames.check: The customer, and the staff or admin.
frames.teach: Those are the actors, and actors are named with a noun. To find them the text gives five questions: who provides input, who receives output, are interfaces required for other systems, are any events triggered automatically at a set time, and who maintains information in the system.
frames.ask: Question three catches the mark most people miss here. Payment is taken and a message is sent. What does that make the payment company?

frames.check: An actor: an external server actor, because it responds to a request from the use case.
frames.teach: There are four types. Primary business actor benefits from it. Primary system actor touches the keyboard and triggers it. External server actor responds to a request. External receiver actor receives output without being primary. The pair that catches people is business against system: the employee benefits from the salary, the bursar dispenses it.
frames.ask: Now the use cases. What rule tells you whether a phrase in the scenario is one?

frames.check: It is something an actor DOES: a verb phrase.
frames.teach: Go through the paragraph and pull out the verbs: create account, log in, view facilities, check availability, make booking, make payment, view, modify, cancel, add facility, set schedule, monitor, generate reports. Each becomes an oval inside a boundary rectangle. Actors stand OUTSIDE the boundary, always, and the boundary must be drawn.
frames.ask: Which two of those happen on EVERY booking, without exception?

frames.check: Check Availability and Make Payment.
frames.teach: Always means include: "Make Booking includes Check Availability". The include exists so common behaviour is written once and reused, and it is drawn as a dashed arrow labelled with the include stereotype.
frames.ask: The scenario also says the customer "can also view, modify, or cancel bookings". Sometimes, not always. What relationship is that, and which way does the arrow point?

frames.check: Extend, and the arrow points FROM the extension TO the base use case.
frames.teach: Say it aloud and the arrow follows the sentence: "Cancel Booking extends Make Booking". Include is always, extend is sometimes, and both are dashed, so direction and label are all you have. Two more relationships exist: depends on, where one use case cannot happen until another has, and generalisation, drawn with a triangle arrowhead, where two actors share behaviour.
frames.ask: The diagram is drawn. The second half asks for a narrative. What is a use case narrative for?

frames.check: It describes step by step how the actor and the system interact to reach the goal.
frames.teach: Seven parts, and the examiner marks them off: name and identifier, actors, description and goal, preconditions, main flow, alternative flows, postconditions. Read it as a story with bookends: preconditions and postconditions are the before and after, the flows are what happens in between.
frames.ask: Which part do students leave out, and which part is the text's own reason use cases are valuable?

frames.check: Alternative flows, and that is exactly the part the text praises.
frames.teach: Use cases are "very helpful for exceptions, special cases and error handling, which developers easily overlook". So write the failure paths: no slot available, payment declined, slot taken while paying. Three lines, and they are the lines that separate a full answer from a half one.

questions.heading: Data flow diagrams, and a campus clinic that keeps losing appointments

scenario.tag: written for practice, in the shape the lecturer confirmed
scenario.text: A university clinic books appointments for students and staff. A patient requests an appointment at the front desk or through the campus portal. The clerk checks the doctor's timetable for a free slot, records the appointment against the patient's file, and gives the patient a slip. On the day, the nurse pulls the patient's file, records the consultation notes the doctor dictates, and where drugs are prescribed sends the prescription to the pharmacy, which records what was dispensed against the same file. At the end of each month the clinic administrator produces a report of attendances by department for the university's health committee.

questions.asked:
PartWhat to writeMarks
(a)The four elements of a data flow diagram: the symbol for each, and the rule for naming each. Then the three process errors and the three illegal data flows, with the fix for each illegal flow7
(b i)Draw the context diagram for the clinic system2.5
(b ii)Draw the Level 0 diagram, showing the major processes and all data stores5
(b iii)Explode ONE process to Level 1, and state how you checked that your diagrams balance3

breakdown.question: What goes on a context diagram that does not go on a Level 0, what goes on a Level 0 that does not go on a context diagram, and how many Level 0 diagrams may this system have?
breakdown.answer:
Context The ENTIRE system as one single process, numbered 0, with the external agents and the flows between them and it. Data stores are usually NOT shown, unless they are owned by another system.

Level 0 The major sub-processes, numbered 1.0, 2.0 and so on, the flows between them, AND the data stores.

How many Exactly one Level 0 per system. Not one per department, not one per process. That is asked directly.

Externals here Patient, Doctor, Pharmacy and the Health Committee. The clerk, nurse and administrator work INSIDE the system, so they are not external agents; their work is the processes.

exam.problem: (a) The four DFD elements with symbols and naming rules, the three process errors, and the three illegal flows with their fixes. (b) For the campus clinic: draw the context diagram, the Level 0 diagram, and a Level 1 explosion of one process, then say how you checked balancing.
exam.answer:
(a) The four elements.

ElementSymbolNamed with
External agent or entityRectangleA descriptive SINGULAR NOUN. It sits outside the boundary and performs no processing
Data flowDirected arrowNOUNS naming the actual information, such as Appointment Request or Prescription
ProcessRectangle with rounded edgesA VERB phrase, and it must not be procedural. "Add 1 to the counter" is wrong; "Increment counter" is right
Data storeOpen ended rectangle, two parallel linesA noun, avoiding verbs and physical descriptions, such as Patient File

The separating phrase: a data store is data at rest, a data flow is data in motion.

The three process errors.

ErrorWhat it looks like
Black holeA process with inputs but no outputs: data goes in and nothing comes out
MiracleA process with outputs but no inputs: data appears from nowhere
Gray holeInputs that are insufficient to produce the outputs shown

The three illegal flows. The rule behind all three is that every data flow must touch at least one process, because if both ends are non process symbols then nothing is doing any work.

Illegal flowThe fix
Data store to data storeInsert a process to MOVE the data from one store to the other
External agent to external agentInsert a process to EXCHANGE the data between the two boundaries
Data store to external agentInsert a process to RETRIEVE and PRESENT the data on the agent's behalf

(b i) The context diagram. One rounded rectangle in the middle, labelled 0 Clinic Appointment System. Four external agent rectangles around it: Patient, Doctor, Pharmacy, Health Committee. No data stores, because none is owned by another system.

Flow inFlow out
Patient: appointment requestPatient: appointment slip
Doctor: timetable, consultation notesDoctor: day's appointment list
Pharmacy: dispensing recordPharmacy: prescription
Health Committee: monthly attendance report

(b ii) The Level 0 diagram. Five processes, numbered, with three data stores. Remember there is exactly one Level 0 diagram per system.

ProcessReadsWrites
1.0 Book AppointmentDoctor Timetable, Patient FileAppointment
2.0 Prepare Day's ClinicAppointment, Patient File
3.0 Record ConsultationPatient FilePatient File
4.0 Issue PrescriptionPatient FilePatient File
5.0 Produce Attendance ReportAppointment, Patient File

Data stores: D1 Patient File, D2 Appointment, D3 Doctor Timetable. External agents: Patient into 1.0 and out of 1.0; Doctor into 3.0 and out of 2.0; Pharmacy out of 4.0 and into 4.0; Health Committee out of 5.0. Note that every store is written by at least one process and read by at least one: a store nothing writes to means a process is missing.

(b iii) Level 1, exploding 1.0 Book Appointment. A Level 1 diagram explodes one process from Level 0, not the whole diagram.

Sub-processWhat it does
1.1 Receive RequestTakes the appointment request from the Patient and identifies the department wanted
1.2 Verify Patient RecordReads Patient File, and creates a record for a first time patient
1.3 Find Free SlotReads Doctor Timetable and returns the available slots
1.4 Record AppointmentWrites the Appointment store and produces the appointment slip for the Patient

How I checked that it balances. Balancing means the inputs and outputs of the higher level process are conserved when it is decomposed. At Level 0, process 1.0 took in the appointment request from the Patient and gave out the appointment slip to the Patient, reading Doctor Timetable and Patient File and writing Appointment. On my Level 1 diagram the appointment request enters 1.1, the appointment slip leaves 1.4, Patient File is read by 1.2, Doctor Timetable is read by 1.3 and Appointment is written by 1.4. The same flows in, the same flows out, the same stores touched, so the diagrams balance and nothing has appeared from nowhere or vanished.

frames.teach: A data flow diagram shows what a system DOES with data: where data comes in, what work is done on it, where it is kept, and where it goes out. The text puts it in one line: the DFD shows the verbs of the system, and the ERD shows the nouns.
frames.ask: Four symbols carry the whole notation. Guess what the four things are, in plain words.

frames.check: Something outside, something that moves, something that does work, something that keeps data.
frames.teach: In order: external agent, a rectangle, named with a singular noun, which does no processing. Data flow, an arrow, named with nouns. Process, a rounded rectangle, named with a verb. Data store, an open ended rectangle, named with a noun and no verbs.
frames.ask: The clerk, the nurse and the administrator all work at the clinic. Are they external agents?

frames.check: No. They work inside the system, so their work IS the processes.
frames.teach: Only the Patient, the Doctor, the Pharmacy and the Health Committee sit outside the boundary. Getting that wrong turns a clean diagram into a crowded one, and it costs marks on every level.
frames.ask: "Add 1 to the counter" is the text's own example of a badly named process. What is wrong with it?

frames.check: It is procedural: it describes HOW a step is coded, not what business function happens.
frames.teach: A DFD is a logical model, so name business functions: Increment counter, Book Appointment, Issue Prescription. Six hints that a thing is a process: it computes, decides, sorts or filters or summarises, organises data into information, triggers other processes, or creates, reads, updates or deletes a stored record.
frames.ask: Now the levels. If the whole system is one process, what is that diagram called, and what is usually missing from it?

frames.check: The context diagram, and data stores are usually left off it.
frames.teach: Context shows the entire system as ONE process with its external agents. Level 0 shows the major sub-processes, their flows and the data stores, and there is exactly one Level 0 per system. Level 1 explodes ONE process from Level 0 into detail.
frames.ask: A process on your diagram has three arrows going in and none coming out. What is that called?

frames.check: A black hole.
frames.teach: Three named errors: black hole, inputs and no outputs; miracle, outputs and no inputs; gray hole, inputs too thin to produce the outputs claimed. Check every process against those three before you hand the paper in.
frames.ask: One rule makes all three illegal flows illegal at once. What must every data flow touch?

frames.check: At least one process.
frames.teach: So store to store, agent to agent and store to agent are all illegal, and each is fixed by inserting a process: one to MOVE data between stores, one to EXCHANGE data between agents, one to RETRIEVE and PRESENT data for an agent.
frames.ask: Last thing, and the single most examined DFD rule. When you explode a process to the next level, what must be conserved?

frames.check: Its inputs and outputs. That is balancing.
frames.teach: Write the balancing sentence into your answer: the request that entered 1.0 enters 1.1, the slip that left 1.0 leaves 1.4, the same stores are touched. It costs ten seconds, it is what the examiner is looking for, and nothing may appear from nowhere or vanish between levels.

questions.heading: Fact finding, and an ERD for a hospital pharmacy

scenario.tag: written for practice, in the shape the lecturer confirmed
scenario.text: A teaching hospital wants a system for its pharmacy. A patient may be prescribed drugs on many visits, and a drug may be prescribed to many patients, so the pharmacy needs to record each individual prescription: which drug, for which patient, on what date, in what dose, and which pharmacist dispensed it. Each prescription is written by one doctor, and a doctor writes many prescriptions. The pharmacy also keeps a record of each drug's stock level and supplier. You have three weeks to gather the requirements. The pharmacists work in shifts and cannot sit in long meetings, the doctors are on ward rounds most of the day, and the pharmacy has four filing cabinets of paper prescriptions going back six years.

questions.asked:
PartWhat to writeMarks
(a)Name the seven fact finding techniques. Then state which two you would use in this hospital and why, and explain what observation uncovers that an interview does not7
(b i)Identify all the entities, including any associative entity needed, and list at least three attributes for each with the identifier marked5
(b ii)Draw the ER diagram, stating the cardinality and the ordinality of every relationship, and name the notation you used5.5

breakdown.question: One phrase in the scenario tells you an associative entity is needed. Which, and what makes a piece of information an entity rather than an attribute?
breakdown.answer:
The phrase "a patient may be prescribed drugs on many visits, and a drug may be prescribed to many patients". That is a many to many, and a many to many is resolved with an associative entity. The scenario then names it: "record each individual prescription".

Entity or attribute An entity is a person, place, object, event or concept the organisation keeps data about, and it always has more than one instance. An attribute is one piece of information about an entity. Dose is an attribute; Prescription has its own identifier, date and dose, so it is an entity.

The fact finding half Shift workers and doctors on rounds mean little time, and four filing cabinets mean the documents already hold the rules. That points at sampling of existing documentation and questionnaires, with short interviews only.

Do not forget The question says state ordinality too, and most answers give only cardinality.

exam.problem: (a) The seven fact finding techniques, the two you would use in this hospital with reasons, and what observation uncovers that an interview does not. (b) For the pharmacy: identify the entities including any associative entity, give three attributes each with identifiers, and draw the ERD with the cardinality and ordinality of every relationship.
exam.answer:
(a) The seven fact finding techniques. Fact finding is the formal process of using research, meetings, interviews, questionnaires, sampling and other techniques to collect information about system problems, requirements and preferences.

  1. Sampling of existing documentation, forms and databases: reviewing organisation charts, memos, standard operating procedures, completed forms, screens and reports, database samples and flowcharts.
  2. Research and site visits: looking outside the organisation at how the problem is solved elsewhere.
  3. Observation of the work environment: the analyst watches or takes part in the work, to learn the system firsthand.
  4. Questionnaires: a special purpose document that collects information and opinions from many respondents quickly and at low cost.
  5. Interviews: collecting information from individuals through face to face interaction.
  6. Prototyping: building a small scale, representative or working model of requirements to discover or verify them.
  7. Joint requirements planning (JRP): highly structured group meetings to analyse problems and define requirements. JRP is a subset of JAD, which covers the whole development process.

The two I would use here, and why.

TechniqueWhy this hospital
Sampling of existing documentationFour filing cabinets of paper prescriptions going back six years are the business rules already written down. Sampling them gives insight into current processes, business rules and information requirements, and it reveals redundancies, inconsistencies and data quality issues, all without taking a minute of a pharmacist's time.
QuestionnairesThe pharmacists work shifts and the doctors are on ward rounds, so a document they answer when free collects information and opinions from many respondents quickly and at low cost. I would use fixed format questions for the facts and a few free format ones for complaints about the present system.

I would keep interviews short and reserve them for the chief pharmacist, using a structured interview with an interview guide, and I would validate the documented responses afterwards.

What observation uncovers that an interview does not. Observation reveals the informal procedures, workarounds, bottlenecks and inefficiencies that users do not mention in interviews. People describe the official process, because that is the one they can put into words and the one they are supposed to follow; observation shows the real one. The guidelines matter: get permission from the supervisor, tell those observed why you are there, keep a low profile, do not interrupt the work, do not focus on trivial activities, do not make assumptions, and take notes during or immediately after, then review them with the people concerned.

(b i) The entities and their attributes. A many to many sits between Patient and Drug, so it is resolved with the associative entity Prescription, which the scenario asks for by name.

PatientDoctorDrugPrescription (associative)
patient_id (identifier)
name
date_of_birth
ward		doctor_id (identifier)
name
specialty
phone_number		drug_code (identifier)
drug_name
stock_level
supplier		prescription_id (identifier)
date_prescribed
dose
dispensed_by

A good identifier should never be blank and should never need to change once assigned, which is why each of these is an assigned code rather than a name or a phone number.

(b ii) The ER diagram. Four rectangles, each relationship drawn as a line through a diamond named with an active verb, and attributes as ovals branching off their entity with the identifier marked. This is Chen notation, which is what the course text uses. If the paper asks for crow's foot instead, the same relationships are drawn with the fork on the many end.

RelationshipRead it both waysCardinalityOrdinality
Patient Receives PrescriptionOne patient receives many prescriptions; each prescription is for exactly one patient1:MA prescription MUST have a patient, so mandatory, minimum one, on that side. A patient may be registered with no prescription yet, so optional, minimum zero, on the other
Doctor Writes PrescriptionOne doctor writes many prescriptions; each prescription is written by exactly one doctor1:MMandatory on the prescription side, optional on the doctor side
Drug Appears On PrescriptionOne drug appears on many prescriptions; each prescription line names one drug1:MMandatory on the prescription side; a drug may sit in stock never prescribed, so optional on the drug side

The point of the associative entity. Patient and Drug are many to many: a patient takes many drugs over time, a drug is given to many patients. Introducing Prescription splits that one many to many into two one to many relationships, which is exactly what an associative entity is for, and it gives the date, dose and dispensing pharmacist a place to live. Without it there is nowhere to record them.

Cardinality against ordinality, since the question asks for both. Cardinality is the MAXIMUM, how many of one relate to the other. Ordinality is the MINIMUM, whether participation is optional, minimum zero, or mandatory, minimum one. Together they say at least this many, at most that many.

frames.teach: Before anything is drawn, the requirements have to be collected, and the course text calls that fact finding: the formal process of using research, meetings, interviews, questionnaires, sampling and other techniques to collect information about problems, requirements and preferences.
frames.ask: You have three weeks, and the staff have almost no free time. Where is the cheapest information in this hospital?

frames.check: The four filing cabinets of paper prescriptions.
frames.teach: That is technique one, sampling of existing documentation, and it costs the user nothing. It gives insight into current processes, business rules and information requirements, and it shows up redundancies, inconsistencies and data quality problems.
frames.ask: The other six are: research and site visits, observation, questionnaires, interviews, prototyping and JRP. Which of them reaches many busy people quickly and cheaply?

frames.check: Questionnaires.
frames.teach: Two formats, and both get asked. Free format gives the respondent latitude: a question, and space to write. Fixed format makes them choose from set responses, in three types: multiple choice, rating and ranking.
frames.ask: Interviews are the obvious technique and they have one blind spot. What will a person never tell you about their own work?

frames.check: The workaround they use instead of the official procedure.
frames.teach: That is why observation exists: it uncovers the informal procedures, workarounds, bottlenecks and inefficiencies users do not mention in interviews. Its rules: permission first, explain why, keep a low profile, do not interrupt, do not assume, take notes at once.
frames.ask: Now the drawing half. An ERD models the data. What is an entity, and why is one named patient not one?

frames.check: An entity is a person, place, object, event or concept the organisation keeps data about, and it always has more than one instance.
frames.teach: So the rectangle is Patient, singular, standing for the whole category. Attributes are ovals hanging off it, and one of them is the identifier, the attribute that uniquely picks out one instance. A good identifier is never blank and never needs to change.
frames.ask: In this pharmacy, can one patient be given many drugs, and can one drug go to many patients?

frames.check: Yes to both.
frames.teach: Yes and yes is a many to many, and a many to many is resolved by introducing an associative entity. Here it is Prescription. The giveaway in an exam question is the phrase "including any associative entity needed": that sentence is telling you a many to many is hiding in the scenario.
frames.ask: Why does Prescription have to be an entity rather than an attribute of something else?

frames.check: Because the date, dose and dispensing pharmacist belong to the pairing, not to the patient or to the drug.
frames.teach: Introducing it turns one many to many into two one to many relationships, which is what makes the model buildable. Name every relationship with an active verb through a diamond, so the diagram reads as a sentence: Patient Receives Prescription.
frames.ask: Ask each relationship in both directions and you get cardinality. What does ORDINALITY add, that most answers leave out?

frames.check: The minimum: whether participation is optional, zero, or mandatory, at least one.
frames.teach: Cardinality is the maximum, ordinality the minimum. A prescription must have a patient, mandatory; a patient may have no prescription yet, optional. Say both for every line, and name your notation: this course text draws Chen, with diamonds and ovals, not crow's foot.

lockin.big: "Module Two is a drawing module. Every artefact has a numbered procedure, and the procedure is the mark scheme."
lockin.sub: Include is always, extend is sometimes and points back to the base. Exactly one Level 0, and balance it. A many to many is resolved with an associative entity, and ordinality is the minimum.
